evergreen_facts.text: Naniwa, on the site of today's Osaka, served more than once as Japan's capital in the 7th and 8th centuries.
In the Edo period Osaka was Japan's great trading center, nicknamed "the nation's kitchen".
The Daisen Kofun near Osaka, a keyhole-shaped burial mound, is attributed to the ancient Emperor Nintoku.
Osaka Castle was built by the warlord Toyotomi Hideyoshi, who began construction in 1583.
Dōtonbori, a canal-side district in Osaka, is known for its neon signs and the giant Glico running man.
Shitennō-ji in Osaka, founded by Prince Shōtoku in 593, is one of Japan's oldest Buddhist temples.
Takoyaki, round balls of batter with chunks of octopus inside, are Osaka's best-known street food.
Okonomiyaki, a savory griddle pancake of batter and cabbage, is a dish closely tied to Osaka.
Sumiyoshi Taisha in Osaka is the head shrine of the many Sumiyoshi shrines found across Japan.
Instant noodles were invented near Osaka by Momofuku Ando, who launched Chicken Ramen in 1958.
Bunraku, Japan's traditional puppet theater, developed in Osaka, home of the National Bunraku Theatre.
Osaka's Tenjin Matsuri, held each July, is one of Japan's three great festivals and ends with a river procession.
Osaka hosted Expo '70, the first world's fair held in Asia, remembered for Tarō Okamoto's Tower of the Sun.
Osaka grew up on Osaka Bay at the mouth of the Yodo River, which drains Lake Biwa.
Osaka is the heart of the Keihanshin region, the metropolitan area it forms with Kyoto and Kobe.
Koshien Stadium, just outside Osaka, hosts Japan's national high school baseball tournaments.
